RW-TTT: Batched Serving for Request-Owned Test-Time Training State
Jian Yang1

Zhizhuo Kou1

Abstract

long context, the model continues learning from
the incoming context, yielding streaming learner
state that changes as the context is processed (Tandon et al., 2025).This state is request-owned: it
must not leak to other requests, and its updates
must follow the backend’s prescribed state transition. A serial TTT path can keep this transition
implicit by processing one stream at a time, but
batched serving must make it explicit. In particular, if a write fails, falls back to a sequential path,
or is rolled back after speculative execution, the
runtime must know which state version remains
valid. We call the resulting tension read-write TTT
serving: READ steps apply request-owned state
without mutation, while WRITE steps update the
state and commit a new version.

Test-time training (TTT) adapts an LLM during generation by reading and updating requestowned state, such as fast weights, low-rank
deltas, or streaming learner state. This breaks
batched LLM serving, which assumes shared
static weights: serial execution is correct but
slow, while naive batching can corrupt request
state. We formulate this problem as read-write
TTT serving and present RW-TTT, which tags
each decode step with its owner, version, and
READ/WRITE effect, batches only compatible phases, and commits updates only to the
owner. On one GPU with eight fast-weight InPlace-TTT streams, RW-TTT reaches 274.61
aggregate tok/s, 9.31× over sequential serving
and 3.44× over per-stream replicas under the
same memory budget. It preserves behavior on
RULER, a long-context benchmark, and passes
owner/version checks.

1

We propose RW-TTT, a serving system for this
setting. RW-TTT tags each serving step with its
owner and READ/WRITE effect, groups only compatible phases into legal batches, executes read
and write operators separately, and commits updates exclusively to the owning requests. To support rollback, failed-write recovery, fallback paths,
and speculative branches, RW-TTT maintains explicit state versions: READ steps preserve version
v, while successful WRITE steps commit version
v + 1. The same contract covers the mutablestate forms above—fast weights, low-rank deltas,
and streaming learner state. The backend supplies
the payload and update rule; RW-TTT supplies
ownership, versioning, rollback-safe commit, and
batch planning. On a long-context serving workload with a fast-weight In-Place-TTT checkpoint,
RW-TTT reaches 274.61 aggregate tok/s, a 9.31×
gain over the sequential TTT path and a 3.44× gain
over naive independent replicas. RULER(Hsieh
et al., 2024) long-context evaluations show that
RW-TTT preserves the adapted checkpoint’s task
behavior.

Introduction

Modern LLM serving batches requests over shared,
read-only weights. vLLM manages dynamic
activation-side state—paged KV cache—but every request still reads the same model parameters (Yu et al., 2022; Kwon et al., 2023; Agrawal
et al., 2023, 2024; Zhong et al., 2024; Zheng et al.,
2024). Adapter-serving systems such as S-LoRA
and Punica add request-specific model-side state,
yet those adapters are pre-existing and read-only
during generation (Sheng et al., 2023; Chen et al.,
2024). Test-time training (TTT) breaks this contract (Sun et al., 2020, 2024; Feng et al., 2026). A
TTT request may carry mutable model-side adaptation state that is both read and updated during
decoding. In In-Place TTT, this state is a set of
request-specific fast weights in the MLP downprojection (Feng et al., 2026). In LoRA-style testtime learning, the mutable state can be represented
as low-rank parameter deltas rather than full-model
updates (Hu et al., 2025). In end-to-end TTT for

The paper makes three contributions.
1

1. A read-write TTT serving contract. We
formulate the serving problem for onlineadaptive TTT checkpoints and define its core
primitives: request ownership, state versions,
READ/WRITE effects, and owner-preserving
commit (§3).

local context. Serving such requests requires two
logical operations:
• READ, which applies the request’s current
state version during token computation; and
• WRITE, which updates the owning request’s
state, typically at chunk boundaries such as
every Cttt generated tokens.

2. An owner/version-aware mutable-state
batching planner. We design a planner that
separates READ and WRITE phases, groups
only compatible next steps, and commits updated versions exclusively to correct request
owners (§4).

Because requests arrive independently and advance
at different rates, one request may be updating its
state while others are still reading earlier state versions. Thus, READ and WRITE operations are not
globally synchronized across requests.

3. End-to-end serving evidence with behavior
and correctness preservation. On the evaluated fast-weight TTT checkpoint, RW-TTT
recovers 9.31× aggregate throughput over the
sequential path while preserving RULER longcontext evaluation (32K/64K) scores and passing owner/version correctness gates. (§5).

2

Background

2.1

Serving with Mutable Model State

2.2

Serving Gap

Table 1 summarizes the gap. Existing runtimes
manage either request-local activation state, as in
KV-cache systems, or immutable request-specific
model-side state, as in adapter-serving systems.
TTT instead requires owned, versioned, mutable
model-side state. Compatible READs can be
batched because they only observe existing versions. WRITEs, however, mutate the owning request’s state and must not become visible to incompatible READs. A TTT serving runtime must therefore track whose state a WRITE updates, which
state version each READ observes, and when an
updated version becomes visible.
A straightforward way to support TTT is to serialize or isolate requests so that READ and WRITE
operations cannot interfere. As shown in Table 2,
these baselines preserve correctness but leave substantial batching opportunities unused. Sequential serving reaches only 29.51 tok/s with eight
streams. Independent replicas improve throughput
to 79.78 tok/s using three batch-1 processes under
∼33 GiB, but still treat requests as isolated executions and therefore cannot share compute across
compatible READ phases.
This leaves the central runtime question: how
can a serving system batch requests with mutable
model-side state while preserving ownership and
version semantics?

Autoregressive serving has two phases: prefill,
which builds the KV cache from the prompt, and
decode, which generates tokens while extending
that cache. Existing serving systems largely rely
on an assumption of immutable model-side state.
• Static-weight serving. Model parameters
are shared across requests and are not modified during generation. This assumption
underlies continuous batching in OrCA (Yu
et al., 2022), paged KV-cache management in
vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023), and structuredgeneration scheduling in SGLang (Zheng
et al., 2024).
• Adapter serving. S-LoRA (Sheng et al.,
2023) and Punica (Chen et al., 2024) batch requests with different adapters (Hu et al., 2022;
Mangrulkar et al., 2022), but each adapter is
fixed during generation.

3

Test-time training (TTT) invalidates this assumption. TTT methods adapt model computation using
inference-time information (Sun et al., 2020, 2024;
Feng et al., 2026). From a serving perspective, the
defining property is request-owned mutable modelside state: each request may carry fast weights,
low-rank deltas, or tail buffers that evolve with its

Serving Model

Read-write TTT serving is the problem of batching
generation requests whose model-side adaptation
state is request-owned and mutable. Given active
requests Rt , the serving system must decide which
next transitions to issue together, and when to issue them, while preserving each request’s owner,

by online mutation.
A request r contains ordinary inference state and
mutable TTT state:

Legal batching. Read and write transitions are
never mixed in the same operator group. More
generally, a group is legal only when its requests
share the same state effect, backend state type, and
operator shape class, and when each request is at
the expected committed version. The backend state
type separates fast-weight TTT, LoRA-style delta
TTT, and streaming learner state. The operator
shape class records the kernel-relevant dimensions
for that backend, such as dtype, layer set, hidden
dimensions, chunk size, rank, or active-row count.
These keys make the batching rule explicit: ordinary activation compatibility is not enough when
requests also read and write private model-side
state.

Ownership. Each mutable TTT state has exactly
one owner. A read transition may consume the
owner’s current state without changing its version:

∀i, j ∈ G : (τi , σi , ρi ) = (τj , σj , ρj ),

where V (ri ) is the serving system’s current committed version for owner ri . The group also carries
an injective owner map: no two batch elements
may commit to the same request-owned state slot
in the same transition. Thus a legal read-write
TTT batch is not merely an activation batch; it is
a group of state-effect-compatible transitions with
valid owner-version bindings.

A write transition consumes backend update evidence ur , produces a new state version, and must
commit that version back to the same owner:
W RITEθ (r, xr , ur , svr ) → (yr , sv+1
r ).
This ownership rule distinguishes TTT state from
shared model weights and from activation-only KV
cache. A serving schedule may reorder independent owners for batching, but it may not redirect,
merge, or alias their mutable states.

(3)

Bounded waiting. The planner may delay a
ready transition to improve compatibility, but only
within a bounded wait budget. If transition e for

Figure 2 places this contract in the serving
stack. Requests carry ordinary KV/cache state plus
TTTState metadata: owner id, backend type, version, placement, and backend metadata. Payloads
such as FastWeightState, DeltaAdapterState,
and TailBufferState represent fast weights,
adapter deltas, and update evidence. A StateView
exposes the executable slice for the next step: read
views are immutable, while write views carry update inputs and mark the candidate state dirty until
commit.
The planner only observes each request’s next
transition. It batches compatible effects and backend shapes automatically, checks that every owner
is at its expected committed version, and uses the
owner map µ to connect physical batch slots back
G
to request semantics. For group G = {rb }B
b=1 with
µ(b) = rb , READ outputs keep all versions unchanged, while WRITE outputs commit only the
owners in µ(G). Selective commit and rollback use
the same owner-indexed state table by snapshotting
cvr ← svr before speculative writes.

Figure 1: Per-request READ/WRITE semantics. Each
decode step evaluates the shared base model with the
request-owned TTT state and exposes either a versionpreserving READ event or a version-creating WRITE
event.

request r becomes ready at decode step tready (r, e)
and is issued at tissue (r, e), then
0 ≤ tissue (r, e) − tready (r, e) ≤ w.

(4)

Thus w = 0 is greedy batching, and finite w bounds
starvation in decode steps while permitting short
phase-alignment waits. Waiting may change which
compatible requests are issued together; it may not
change an individual request’s read/write order or
update rule.
Correctness contract. The target behavior is the
original sequential TTT execution using the same
backend and update rule. An execution schedule is
behavior-preserving if it preserves request-output
mapping, read-step immutability, write order and
count, version progression, owner-local commit,
and tail/cache consistency for every request. In
experiments, we validate this semantic contract
through owner/version/tail invariants and by checking that per-token NLL and task scores match the
sequential TTT reference within the reported tolerance. This is the serving contract: RW-TTT
changes the execution plan, not the adapted TTT
semantics.

CONTROL. C OMMIT /ROLLBACK controls visibility. Commit publishes a dirty state as owner r’s
next version only after the WRITE group succeeds;
rollback restores the checkpointed owner slot and
version; fork creates a separate owner/version lineage. The version counter changes here, not inside
the backend update, and only owner-indexed TTT
records are modified.

Backend Instantiations

This interface lets multiple TTT styles share
the same serving contract. A backend exposes
a request-owned payload, immutable read view,
write evidence for its update rule, compatibility
metadata (backend type, operator shape, and placement), and commit metadata for the owner slot
and candidate version. The runtime uses only this
interface; the backend retains its learning formula.
For example, a fast-weight backend stores mutable fast weights in FastWeightState; a LoRAstyle backend stores request-owned low-rank deltas

Evidence scope. We separate throughput measurement from behavior validation. The throughput harness measures scheduler-inclusive aggregate
tok/s under controlled traces. Full task behavior is
evaluated on RULER-32K/64K (Hsieh et al., 2024),
because throughput measurement and long-context
task execution answer different validation questions. Mutable-state correctness is further validated
by numerical gates and contract stress tests (§5.5).

Evaluation

We organize the evaluation around five questions:
❶ Is the sequential serving collapse caused by
mutable-state batching rather than per-request TTT
cost? ❷ How much one-GPU serving capacity does
RW-TTT recover? ❸ Does RW-TTT preserve the
adapted checkpoint’s long-context behavior? ❹ Do
owner or version correctness checks hold under
numerical and state-contract tests? ❺ How broadly
does the same read-write contract apply beyond the
headline trace?

5.2

Batching Bottleneck Diagnosis

We first isolate single-request overhead from batching loss. The measured RW-TTT single-request
overhead is small, so the sequential serving collapse is primarily a batching failure.
Controlled batch-1 timing shows that
RW-TTT’s per-request execution overhead
is modest: median 1.4% total, 2.1% prefill, and
0.4% decode. The serving bottleneck is therefore
the inability to safely batch request-owned mutable
streams. The sequential path yields only 29.51
tok/s for eight concurrent requests because it
serializes all mutable-state effects.

Experimental Setup and Evidence Scope

We evaluate a Qwen3-4B In-Place-TTT fastweight checkpoint (Yang et al., 2025; Feng et al.,
2026). Headline serving results use one GPU,
BF16 cached decode, eight request-private CUDA
streams, 4096 prompt tokens, 512 decode tokens,
and TTT chunk size 128. We report schedulerinclusive aggregate generated-token throughput,
including grouping, waiting, fallback, and state
movement.

5.3

GPU Serving Throughput

We next measure aggregate throughput under the
one-GPU memory class. RW-TTT recovers most
of the lost serving capacity and remains effective
under higher write pressure.

comparisons. The full RW-TTT path achieves
274.61 tok/s: 9.31× over the sequential path and
3.44× over memory-matched replicas. The uni-

Long-Context Behavior Preservation

We then check whether executing the adapted
checkpoint through RW-TTT changes longcontext task behavior. We compare against the original In-Place TTT path. Table 5 reports full RULER
evaluation scores. The same adapted checkpoint
is executed by the original In-Place TTT path and
by RW-TTT on RULER, a 13-task long-context
evaluation suite (Hsieh et al., 2024). The 32K score
is essentially unchanged (76.41 vs. 76.30) and the
64K score is identical (67.72), with the full per-task
breakdown retained in Appendix D.

Speedup over PyTorch eager

5.6

Operator Evidence

Finally, we look beyond the headline 4K serving
trace. The same contract survives breadth sweeps,
exposes the 16K memory boundary, carries a second adapter-shaped mutable state, and identifies
WRITE-side operator targets.
Figure 4 provides local evidence for the readwrite operator surface induced by mutable TTT
state. Triton kernels reduce WRITE-side latency
for selective commit, dense update, and checkpoint
write by 3.1×, 2.5×, and 1.2×, respectively. These
microbenchmarks are not the end-to-end serving
denominator; they show that the unusual optimization surface lies in owner-indexed commit, state
update, and checkpointing rather than ordinary
shared-weight projection.

Correctness Checks

We combine task scores, calibrated numerical gates,
and explicit state-contract stress tests to check the
owner/version contract. All three evidence layers
support the same correctness conclusion, showing
in Table 6.
These layers address complementary failure
7

6

Discussion

Adapter serving. S-LoRA and Punica make heterogeneous request-specific model-side state a firstclass serving concern (Hu et al., 2022; Sheng
et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Mangrulkar et al.,
2022). Their core contract is read-side heterogeneity: different requests apply different low-rank
weights, and the serving stack manages placement
and batched execution, but adapters remain readonly during generation. Read-write TTT builds on
the same insight that small request-specific model
state can be served efficiently, then adds online mutation: a LoRA-style TTT state can be read like
an adapter, dirtied by an update event, committed
under a new version, and read again by the same
request. Our LoRA-style stress test confirms that
the same serving interface carries adapter-shaped
payloads.

Phase skew remains hard. Requests are not
fixed as boundary or non-boundary streams; each
stream alternates between READ and WRITE
steps. When updates align, the planner forms dense
WRITE batches, but phase skew fragments groups.
The bounded wait budget trades latency for group
density without changing semantics, leaving skewaware scheduling as future work.
State movement and layout. Read-write TTT
shifts the serving surface from shared-weight projection to mutable-state commit, checkpoint, and
movement. State packing and ownership tracking
grow with the number of owners, making state layout and memory management the next bottleneck
after batching is restored.

Test-time training. Test-time training adapts
models using information available at inference
time (Sun et al., 2020). Recent work uses test-time
learning inside recurrent-style hidden states (Sun
et al., 2024), while In-Place-TTT applies online updates to selected LLM layers during long-context
generation (Feng et al., 2026). These are backend choices for producing mutable state and update
rules. RW-TTT targets the missing serving-system
layer needed when such methods read and write
request-owned state during generation.

Operator kernels. Microbenchmarks show local
wins for selective commit and dense update operators, while read-path projection does not beat
torch.bmm. Thus WRITE-side kernelization is a
targeted follow-up, not a substitute for the serving
contract.
Validation scope. Our full validation uses fastweight In-Place-TTT checkpoints, which provide
a sequential reference and long-context RULER
tasks. The LoRA-style experiment tests the same
owner/version contract on adapter-shaped payloads,
but is not a full downstream adapter-serving evaluation.

7

8

Conclusion

Test-time training introduces request-owned mutable model state that breaks the static-weight batching contract behind current LLM serving systems.
RW-TTT restores batching through a read-write
serving contract: each decode step is tagged with
its owner and READ/WRITE effect, only compatible phases are grouped, and updated state versions are committed exclusively to owning requests.
On eight concurrent streams with a fast-weight InPlace-TTT checkpoint, this recovers 274.61 aggregate tok/s—9.31× over the sequential TTT
path and 3.44× over memory-matched independent replicas—while preserving adapted RULER32K/64K behavior and passing owner/version correctness gates. The contribution is a serving contract and batching runtime for request-owned mutable state, not a new TTT learning rule or kernel
system; RW-TTT separates TTT backend design
from the serving semantics needed to batch onlineadaptive model state.

Related Work

KV/prefix-cache serving. Modern LLM serving has optimized the shared-weight contract
through iteration-level scheduling (Yu et al., 2022),
paged KV-cache management (Kwon et al., 2023),
chunked-prefill/decode overlap (Agrawal et al.,
2023, 2024), prefill/decode disaggregation (Zhong
et al., 2024), program-level scheduling and cache
reuse (Zheng et al., 2024), and further refinements
in high-throughput generation, co-serving, and
elastic disaggregation (Holmes et al., 2024; Qiao
et al., 2024; Ruan et al., 2025; Borui et al., 2025).
These systems manage dynamic activation-side
state while model-side parameters remain shared
and read-only. RW-TTT keeps the scheduling
problem but changes the object being scheduled:
each request also owns model-side state whose version may change during generation.
8

Limitations

Cheng-Ping Hsieh, Simeng Sun, Samuel Kriman, Shantanu Acharya, Dima Rekesh, Fei Jia, Yang Zhang,
and Boris Ginsburg. 2024. Ruler: What’s the real
context size of your long-context language models?
arXiv preprint arXiv:2404.06654.

RW-TTT evaluates the serving layer for existing
online TTT behavior rather than proposing a new
adaptation rule. We therefore hold the backend
update rule fixed and ask whether request-owned
mutable state can be batched without changing the
adapted checkpoint’s behavior. Full task evaluation uses the fast-weight In-Place-TTT checkpoints
because they provide both a sequential reference
and long-context adapted checkpoints; the LoRAstyle experiment exercises the same owner/version
READ/WRITE contract on adapter-shaped mutable state. The throughput ladder is reported for the
one-GPU memory class and eight-stream workload
used by the prototype, with comparisons against the
original sequential TTT path and memory-matched
unmodified TTT replicas. Static-weight serving
is a different contract: RW-TTT targets the case
where model-side request state is read and written
during generation.

Reproducibility Notes

We distinguish three throughput scopes. Decode-only counts only the decode execution window after
prompt state is available. Prefill+decode also includes prompt processing. Scheduler-inclusive further
includes grouping, waiting, fallback, and state movement. The main-text serving rows use one canonical
scheduler-inclusive scope; other scopes appear only in the appendix denominator map.

Under 16384 prompt tokens and 512 decode tokens with 7 concurrent streams:

PEFT/LoRA Adapter-State Path Check

The LoRA-style experiment maps rank-8 PEFT adapter states to DeltaAdapterState and exercises the
same ownership, versioning, READ/WRITE, and commit path used by fast-weight TTT state. This is an
interface and path check, not a downstream LoRA-TTT quality benchmark.
Four materialized adapter/domain pairs are tested. All pass exact apply/update operator equivalence
checks with adapter-file NLL changes below 3.4×10−3 , confirming that the mutable-state serving contract
carries a second payload shape without corruption.

G

Operator Microbench Details

The read-write serving contract fixes the operator boundary: READ steps consume a versioned state view;
WRITE steps compute updated state and commit it. On representative H800 BF16 shapes (Qwen3-4B
dimensions), Triton kernels show WRITE-side opportunities:

management, wait-budget logic, and fallback handling.
